title: Root Vegetable Gratin
subtitle: thinly sliced potato, celeriac, and carrot in cream and gruyere
excerpt: A gratin of root vegetables is one of the most satisfying winter dishes. Thinly sliced potato, celeriac, and carrot are layered with cream, garlic, and thyme, then topped with gruyere and baked until tender and golden. It serves 6 as a generous side.
sourceNotes: Based on the French gratin dauphinois tradition from the Dauphine region. The addition of celeriac and carrot is a British home-cooking adaptation that adds colour and a slightly sweeter flavour.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble up to a day ahead. Bake from chilled, adding 15 minutes to the cooking time.

content.text: Slice all the vegetables as thinly and evenly as possible -- about 3mm. A mandoline makes this quick. Uneven slices mean some will overcook while others are still firm.
Preheat the oven to 180C. Butter a large gratin dish generously.
Mix the cream, milk, garlic, thyme, and nutmeg in a bowl. Season with salt and pepper.
Layer the vegetables in the dish, alternating potato, celeriac, and carrot. Season between each layer.
Pour the cream mixture over the top, pressing the vegetables down gently. It should just cover them.
Scatter the gruyere over the top. Cover tightly with foil.
Bake for 50 minutes. Remove the foil and bake for another 20 minutes until the top is golden and the vegetables are completely tender.

items.symptom: Vegetables still firm after full baking time
items.cause: Sliced too thick or foil not sealed tightly
items.fix: Cover tightly and add 15 more minutes. Check with a thin knife -- it should slide through with no resistance.

items.symptom: Top burnt before vegetables are cooked
items.fix: Cover again with foil and lower the heat by 10 degrees.

content.text: The gratin dauphinois comes from the Dauphine region of southeastern France and has been made there since at least the 18th century. The original is potato only, cooked in cream with garlic. The addition of other root vegetables is a British adaptation that adds colour and a slightly sweeter character. It remains one of the great cold-weather side dishes.
